The dynamic reverses because Sitaram, who previously refused to fight against Udayaditya and begged for mercy citing his past debts, eventually helps free Udayaditya by breaking into locked doors with force upon hearing a fire alarm; in the process of escaping himself later, he admits that even after being beaten, it is "the Yubaraj [Udayaditya] has escaped," indicating that Udayaditya now holds Sitaram's loyalty completely.

Pratapaditya's initial plan was for two Pathan men (Muktiyar Khan and his brother) to assassinate Basanta Ray while he took shelter at an inn in Simultali on his way to Jessore. The method that finally succeeded involved Muktiyar Khan capturing Udayaditya, then returning alone to the fort under cover of evening prayers where he executed Basanta Ray by beheading him after receiving a signed death order from Pratapaditya.
1. Disguised as a woman named Ramai Thakur (in Vibha's bedchamber/inner quarters) and 2. Disguised as Rammohan's "dada" or uncle (Ramai Bhand, the jester).

Rukmini (who had changed her name to Mangala) prepared a poison using various roots while chanting mantras so that Pratapaditya would have no pity for Surma; this secret stipend and the act of poisoning caused Surma's departure.
Vibha arrives at her husband's palace on time for a welcoming ceremony only to discover that he has already married someone else and received another wife because of Vibha's delay.

Udayaditya's signet ring ends up being used as evidence against him because Rukmini gives the forged petition, which was created using a seal derived from that ring (or bearing his name), directly to Pratapaditya. Bhagavat intercepts and delivers this document to the Maharaj, where it is presented as a treasonous complaint lodged by Udayaditya against himself with the Emperor. Although the minister argues that such an act of treason is unbelievable, Pratapaditya orders Udayaditya's imprisonment based on the accusation contained in the forged petition.

Ramchandra Ray's escape triggers an investigation into why the dismissed guards (Sitaram and Bhagavat) were receiving secret monthly stipends from Surma instead of their usual salaries; when Pratapaditya learns that Udayaditya orchestrated these payments, he believes this act constitutes a major crime against him. Fueled by rage over perceived insolence rather than simple financial matters, the Maharaja issues an order demanding that both Urdayaditya's wife Surma be exiled to her paternal home to appease his anger and assert his authority.

The song "I alone am left behind" signifies profound loneliness and emptiness caused by the loss of loved ones who have passed away or moved on, leaving only desolation for the singer. Basanta Ray sings it in two contrasting contexts: first, while sitting alone at his palace veranda gazing at a setting sun, reflecting with melancholy thoughts that those he used to sing for are no longer there; and second, after visiting Vibha's room which is now silent and empty because her family members are gone or imprisoned, where he sings the song in desolation before taking her hand.

Udayaditya failed Rukmini by escaping without her consent, which led Basanta Ray to hide him from his father instead of returning as ordered. This disobedience made Udayaditya decide to secretly escape again; while planning this final flight alone outside the palace, he was captured and taken before Muktiyar Khan to be executed on Pratapaditya's orders (which stipulated that Basanta Ray could also die if Udayaditya escaped).

Pratapaditya receives Ramchandra with cold indifference and without joy or haste, while Ramchandra later addresses Pratapaditya's status by asserting that marrying into his family is sufficient to redeem seven generations, yet simultaneously mocking him for lowering their noble house by taking a daughter who no longer belongs to her father after marriage.

The older widow from Raigarh (named Rukmini or Mangala) re-enters Udayaditya's life by changing her name and living on the outskirts of Jessore; she befriends palace servants to gather news, uses magic and tantric rituals hoping for the death of his wife Surma so she can win his heart, eventually appearing in a stormy night offering false affection after losing her wealth and social status.

Udayaditya's lament culminates in a formal renunciation of the throne when he approaches his father with an unwavering determination to refuse rule over Jessore. He explicitly states that if believed, he will take an oath before Ma-Kali and swear not to accept even a needle's tip worth of land or sit on the throne as long as he lives. To prove this renunciation is genuine rather than self-serving, he voluntarily gives up his kingdom to make Samaraditya heir instead. Furthermore, he pleads for release from imprisonment like a "caged beast" and requests funds to build a guest house and temple in Kashi under the name of his murdered grand-uncle. He formally seals this renunciation by swearing that if he ever touches Jessore's royal scepter again, all sin related to his grandfather's murder would fall upon him; after taking this oath before his father at the temple, he leaves for Kashi with a letter from his mother in hand, effectively abandoning royalty and family life.

Ramchandra Ray's letter is intercepted by the old man named Nayanchand, who fears the consequences if it reaches Pratapaditya and instead gives it to the Mahishi (Udayaditya's mother). The Mahishi then shows the letter only to Basanta Ray. She does not show it directly to Vibha because she believes the delicate Vibha could not survive hearing about it. Furthermore, when asked by Vibha why Udayaditya has abandoned her or if he wrote such a letter, the family instead announces that Ramchandra *has* written requesting Vibha be sent back and claims his anger will subside once she is sent to Chandradwip, thereby hiding the actual angry content of the intercepted letter from Vibha.

Pratapaditya fails to trap Ramchandra Ray because Rammohan and his followers managed to pull the boat up and over the large sal wood logs that were blocking the canal before the guards could bring their own chase boat. The delay in bringing a pursuit vessel was caused by a boat-caller who stopped at Harimudi's shop to smoke tobacco instead of rushing immediately, which allowed the escaping party to reach the Bhairav river where Fernandez fired a cannon.

The relationship with his sitar reflects Basanta Ray's growing despair because the instrument had long been his "eternal companion," but now that he must leave Udayaditya and cannot reach them due to prison walls, the situation renders him utterly alone. Initially struggling to play furiously while crying so hard his throat choked, he eventually declares that only an emptiness remains; later in Raigarh, he tells Khan Saheb that although his physical sitar still exists, its strings have broken and it can no longer be tuned, symbolizing that the music which once defined his joy is lost to him. This loss of his companion signifies that without Udayaditya and Surma, there are "no more joys" left for him or anyone else in Raigarh.

Before Surma's death, Udayaditya was willing to stop injustice immediately without hesitation (e.g., rushing out to save subjects being beaten or looted), but after her death and due to his fear of Pratapaditya, he hesitated in every task regarding the oppressed, did not send money despite wishing to help, refused orders to take action against oppression, and allowed suffering to continue.

Sitaram ultimately undoes the specific damage he caused by conspiring with Bhagavat when a fire breaks out near Udayaditya's prison; during the chaos, Sitaram finds Yubaraj (Udayaditya) and leads him through the escape route to safety after realizing that the guards had fled their posts.

Rammohan physically extracts members of the royal family (Ramchandra Ray) from hostile palaces twice using a rope made of tied-together sheets and climbing down it from the palace roof to escape into a canal below; in this specific instance, he ties Ramchandra to his back but carefully releases him onto the boat just before jumping himself.

Vibha initially appeared fully adorned for royalty in Jessore, wearing eight thick gold bangles and a huge diamond bracelet instead of her preferred turquoise ones, sporting an oversized nose ring despite it not suiting her delicate face, suffering from an elaborate hairstyle she secretly disliked but was forced to wear again after her maidservant ruined it. She felt joyous and flustered by this extravagant presentation. In contrast, when she finally sought him out in Chandradwip seeking Ramchandra Ray after learning he had married elsewhere, she dressed as a common beggar-woman without any palanquin or finery, entered the palace like a servant rather than a queen, was immediately unrecognized and treated with disdain by those who ignored her plea to give away everything into his hands for another's wife.

In the bedchamber after Surma's death, the window represents an empty seat that highlights her absence; Udayaditya sits there hoping against hope for a voice like hers or to see someone sitting at that spot where she used to sit. In contrast, during his time in prison, the small sliver of sky and light visible through the tiny window becomes the only patch of land where he feels naturally free; it symbolizes his future liberation and breaks the darkness around him, making the room itself feel like a true cage rather than a place of freedom.

The dynamic devolves into a life-threatening encounter when Sitaram returns to Rukmini's house after discovering the Yubaraj has escaped, intending to strangle her for potentially exposing his conspiracy; upon finding her shivering in fear of death following her curse against him and seeking revenge on their mutual enemies.

Sitaram's strategy evolves by actively manipulating the situation after Udayaditya escapes through the prison fire he secretly started. Instead of allowing the truth to surface, Sitaram spreads false news claiming the Yubaraj died in the collapse and burning flames; his men set a specific room ablaze, throw bones and the sword inside to create confusion, and report that screams were heard only before they announce the roof collapsed with no response found. This fabricated death narrative successfully distracts everyone from investigating Udayaditya's actual escape route, allowing Sitaram to flee Jessore immediately afterward while the official story of his execution solidifies in the court until Rukmini reveals it as a conspiracy by Pratapaditya and the old king.

In his court, Ramchandra Ray interprets Udayaditya's behavior as futile resistance against a plan where Pratapaditya intended to sell Vibha (his daughter) after she became a widow; furthermore, he dismisses the act of saving him not out of genuine gratitude or duty but rather believing it was done solely for Udayaditya's own sister and that Ramchandra should have felt pain if anyone else were in danger. Ultimately, despite Udayaditya ignoring his peril to save Ramchandra's life, Ray mocks the incident at court without remorse due to his fickle nature, small-mindedness, fear of ridicule from flatterers like Ramai Bhand, and a lack of true gratitude.

The political specter of the Emperor of Delhi becomes the mechanism used to imprison his son because a forged petition, falsely accusing Prince Udayaditya (the Yubaraj) of treason against Pratapaditya with an intent for him to seize the kingdom himself, is written and stamped. This document is delivered by Bhagavat under the pretense that it was intended for the Emperor in Delhi; upon reading this false accusation, Pratapaditya reacts angrily but effectively uses the perceived threat of the Emperor's displeasure as justification or context for his son's subsequent imprisonment or punishment, having already ordered guards to be summoned.

Vibha's hair becomes a marker of Surma's presence and subsequent tragic absence when Vibha initially goes secretly to Surma to have her hair styled, which causes the Mahishi to realize that "Surma... had purposely ruined [the hairstyle]" out of jealousy. Later, after Surma is gone, Vibha sits quietly waiting for Surma to come and braid her hair; however, since Surma does not return, her hair remains unbraided until many days pass, symbolizing the companionless sorrow Vibha suffers in Surma's absence.
